query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A pulse‐modulated laser scanning strategy with reduced pulse durations and tailored inter‐pulse dwell times will induce a nonequilibrium short‐range order during solidification in AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, thereby reducing residual thermal stresses and enhancing mechanical properties compared to conventional high-thermal-load regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed under high-thermal-load LPBF conditions, which typically exhibit steep thermal gradients, significant residual stresses, and microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Implement a pulse‐modulated laser scanning regime with approximately 30% reduced pulse durations (e.g., 50 µs pulse with 150 µs dwell time) during laser powder bed fusion.
generation.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion of sub-centimeter miniature components under ambient build chamber conditions, employing the specified pulsing parameters.
generation.structural_mediator: Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order (SRO) established during rapid solidification.
generation.mechanism: The reduced energy per pulse and extended dwell times lower thermal gradients during solidification, promoting a more uniform atomic arrangement via nonequilibrium SRO formation at grain boundaries. This uniformity is expected to alleviate localized residual stresses and reduce microstructural defects linked to high thermal loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components processed with the pulse-modulated strategy will exhibit lower residual stresses, improved yield and fatigue strengths, and a more homogenized microstructure relative to those fabricated with conventional continuous high-energy scanning.
generation.baseline: Components manufactured using standard high-energy continuous laser scanning that produce high thermal gradients, resulting in significant residual stresses and microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to miniature components (sub-centimeter dimensions) processed by LPBF using the specified pulsed regime; its effectiveness for larger or bulk components and under alternative manufacturing parameters is not established.
generation.uncertainty: The precise tuning of pulse and dwell times necessary to reproducibly induce the desired SRO is challenging, and the complete influence of induced SRO on all relevant mechanical properties in this specific alloy system remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two LPBF fabrication campaigns on AlCrFeNiSi powder: one employing the proposed pulse-modulated laser strategy (50 µs pulse with 150 µs dwell time) and another using conventional continuous scanning. Both sets should use identical miniature component geometries and ambient conditions. Post-fabrication, subject samples to residual stress measurements, mechanical testing, and microstructural characterization.
measurements: Residual stress distribution via X-ray diffraction
Yield strength and fatigue performance through standard mechanical tests
Atom probe tomography or high-resolution diffraction to assess the presence and distribution of nonequilibrium SRO
SEM analysis of microstructure and crack densities
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components processed with the pulse-modulated regime do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses, improvement in mechanical properties, or measurable differences in SRO compared with the conventionally processed components, the hypothesis is falsified.

To achieve this, we devise two distinct LPBF processing strategies denoted as “H” and “L” (detailed in “Methods”) to produce SS316L with high and low thermal stability, respectively. During LPBF, a thin layer of metal powders is spread over a build platform and then selectively melted by a high-power laser source (Fig. 1a). Melting occurs sequentially as the laser is scanned back and forth in tracks that fill the areas to be consolidated. The H and L strategies differ in how close melt tracks are to one another within a single layer (i.e., the melt track area density), which is determined by the hatch spacing parameter, h. They also differ in how many times the same layer is scanned by the laser; namely whether the previously consolidated material is remelted or not. The complex temperature cycle in L-PBF with a rapid cooling rate can cause thermal residual stress in the solidification substructure, which induces cracks. To further investigate the characteristics of the printed sample, the microstructure was characterized by SEM and EDX analyses, as shown in Figure 5a,b. Intergranular and transgranular cracks were observed in the printed sample. EDX analysis showed furthermore that the cracks were irregular, and their size was in the range from tens to hundreds of micrometers (Figure 5a,b). Quantitative analysis of the SEM images revealed that the average crack density decreased from 12.3 cracks/mm2 at a VED of 251.2 J/mm3 to 4.3 cracks/mm2 at a VED of 187.7 J/mm3, while the maximum observed crack length also decreased from 193.3 μm to 84.2 μm over the same range. This trend demonstrates a clear inverse relationship between VED and both crack density and crack length, consistent with findings in the literature that higher energy input can increase thermal gradients and residual stresses, thereby promoting crack formation, while lower VEDs may reduce cracking but risk lack of fusion or porosity. AbstractMetallic alloys are routinely subjected to nonequilibrium processes during manufacturing, such as rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. It has been suggested in the high-entropy alloy literature that chemical short-range order (SRO) could offer a new knob to tailor materials properties. While evidence of the effect of SRO on materials properties accumulates, the state of SRO evolution during alloy manufacturing remains obscure. Here, we employ high-fidelity atomistic simulations to track SRO evolution during the solidification and thermomechanical processing of alloys. Our investigation reveals that alloy processing can lead to nonequilibrium steady-states of SRO that are different from any equilibrium state. The mechanism behind nonequilibrium SRO formation is shown to be an inherent ordering bias present in nonequilibrium events. These results demonstrate that conventional manufacturing processes provide pathways for tuning SRO that lead to a broad nonequilibrium spectrum of SRO states beyond the equilibrium design space of alloys.Subject terms: Atomistic models, Metals and alloys This study reveals that traditional manufacturing can create nonequilibrium

proposals.material_system: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature AM components
proposals.intervention: Implement a pulse‐modulated laser scanning strategy that imposes controlled, lower-energy pulses designed to promote nonequilibrium chemical short-range order (SRO) during solidification
proposals.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion using pulse durations reduced by ~30% from conventional settings, with inter-pulse dwell times adjusted (e.g. pulses of 50 µs with 150 µs off-time) on miniature components (sub-centimeter dimensions) at ambient build chamber conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Nonequilibrium SRO developed during tailored rapid solidification
proposals.mechanism: The pulsed energy input creates milder thermal gradients that enable the formation of a beneficial SRO state. This state relieves local stresses by promoting more uniform atomic arrangements at grain boundaries, in contrast to the high thermal load regime that induces residual stresses and microstructural heterogeneity
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to components produced with conventional high-thermal-load regimes, the treated parts are expected to exhibit lower residual stress, enhanced yield and fatigue strength, and reduced processing complexity due to a more homogenized microstructure
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly targets thermal gradients and rapid cooling kinetics, using nonequilibrium SRO as a mediator to both relax residual thermal stresses and improve mechanical properties, while simplifying process complexities by eliminating the need for subsequent stress-relief treatments

proposals.material_system: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature AM components
proposals.intervention: Introduce an in situ pre-heating of the build platform using induction heating integrated into the LPBF system
proposals.conditions: Maintain the powder bed at an elevated temperature (e.g., 350–400°C) during the build of miniature components (dimensions <1 cm³) under otherwise identical LPBF parameters
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients across the melt pool and part
proposals.mechanism: Pre-heating the build platform reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and the surrounding material. This minimizes rapid cooling and thermal shock, thereby reducing residual thermal stresses and promoting a uniform microstructure with balanced recrystallization kinetics
proposals.predicted_outcome: The resulting components are anticipated to display significantly lowered residual stresses, improved ductility and mechanical performance, and a simplified process without the need for post-build annealing
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By controlling the in situ thermal environment through pre-heating, the intervention overcomes the drawbacks of high thermal loads during conventional AM, reducing stress accumulation and enhancing microstructural uniformity in a single processing step

proposals.material_system: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature AM components
proposals.intervention: Apply an integrated dual-laser system where a secondary low-power laser provides localized in situ thermal annealing immediately after melt pool formation
proposals.conditions: During LPBF, a primary laser forms the part while a preprogrammed secondary laser, operating at ~20% power with a dwell time of a few milliseconds per scan track, scans the freshly solidified material in miniature components (sub-cm geometries) under inert atmosphere
proposals.structural_mediator: Localized thermal annealing zones that promote stress relaxation and microstructural homogenization
proposals.mechanism: The secondary laser temporarily elevates the temperature of the near-solidified regions, enabling a controlled annealing effect that mitigates residual stresses and refines grain boundaries without inducing overall high thermal loads. This dual-laser approach synergistically fuses melting and in situ annealing in one process
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional builds, components processed with this dual-laser intervention are expected to exhibit a marked reduction in residual stress, enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and fatigue resistance), and a lower degree of microstructural heterogeneity
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single, process-integrated intervention cleverly combines melting and stress-relief, directly addressing the issues of thermal stress and degraded mechanical properties without resorting to complex post-processing

proposals.material_system: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature AM components
proposals.intervention: Implement laser beam shaping to convert the typical Gaussian beam profile into a flat-top profile to achieve uniform energy distribution and reduced peak thermal gradients
proposals.conditions: Adapt the LPBF system with a beam shaping module that produces a flat-top profile at a laser power reduced by approximately 20% relative to standard settings and increased scanning speed to maintain constant energy input, applied to fabricating miniature components (<1 cm³) at standard LPBF environmental conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: A uniformly distributed melt pool with reduced thermal gradients
proposals.mechanism: By transforming the beam profile to a flat-top shape, the local energy input becomes more uniform across the melt pool area. This minimizes hotspots and extreme thermal gradients that contribute to residual stress formation. The resulting uniform cooling promotes a consistent microstructure with fewer defects
proposals.predicted_outcome: Parts produced with this beam shaping technique are predicted to have lower populations of residual stresses and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., improved yield strength and ductility) compared to components fabricated under conventional Gaussian laser regimes
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention offers a single, equipment-based modification that directly mitigates the thermal gradients inherent in high-thermal-load AM methods, thus overcoming processing complexity and stress-related degradation

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposal directly tackles the issue by reducing thermal gradients with a pulsed laser regime, promoting nonequilibrium SRO which is hypothesized to relieve residual stresses and improve mechanical properties.
critiques.constraints: The intervention specifically targets AlCrFeNiSi in miniature components under LPBF conditions with modified pulsing and dwell times; it respects the constraints but relies on precise control over ultrashort pulse parameters.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; modulating the energy input can affect rapid solidification dynamics and promote a beneficial SRO state, as supported by nonequilibrium alloy studies.
critiques.feasibility: Pulse‐modulated laser strategies are established in laser processing, though achieving the appropriate pulse/dwell time window to consistently form the desired SRO may be challenging.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC12508472 suggests that nonequilibrium SRO can be induced during rapid solidification, and PMC12250662 supports the role of thermal gradients in crack formation.
critiques.main_risk: Fine-tuning the pulse duration and dwell times to achieve the desired SRO without introducing other defects is challenging, and the effect of SRO in this specific alloy system is not yet fully validated.
critiques.fix: Incorporate a detailed falsification experiment plan that quantitatively measures SRO (e.g., via atom probe tomography or diffraction techniques) to directly correlate pulse parameters with microstructural outcomes.

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposal mitigates residual thermal stresses by pre-heating the build platform, reducing the temperature gradient during processing.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system and processing window for miniature components under LPBF, although the pre-heating temperature must be carefully controlled to avoid unwanted microstructural coarsening or oxidation.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is well-established; elevating the build platform temperature is known to lower thermal gradients and associated residual stress in additive manufacturing.
critiques.feasibility: In situ platform heating is a standard technique and is feasible with current LPBF systems, though integration with miniature component builds requires calibration.
critiques.evidence: Supporting evidence from PMC12348559 and PMC11807212 shows that pre-heating can reduce cracking and improve microstructural uniformity.
critiques.main_risk: The chosen temperature range (350–400°C) might be suboptimal (or too high) compared to other studies, risking unwanted grain growth or oxidation, and the thermal gradient may not be sufficiently minimized for this specific alloy.
critiques.fix: Refine the pre-heating temperature based on detailed thermal simulations and preliminary experiments to optimize stress reduction while safeguarding microstructural integrity.

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposal aims to overcome residual stresses and microstructural degradation by using a secondary laser for localized in situ thermal annealing, thus directly targeting stress relief.
critiques.constraints: While it applies to the AlCrFeNiSi system and miniature components, integrating a dual-laser setup may conflict with the goal of reducing processing complexity, as it adds extra hardware complexity.
critiques.physical_soundness: The concept of localized re-heating to relieve stresses is physically sound; however, ensuring precise synchronization between the two lasers is nontrivial and may lead to non-uniform effects.
critiques.feasibility: Although dual-laser systems have been explored, integrating them into an already complex LPBF machine for miniature components may be challenging and less mature compared to single-laser modifications.
critiques.evidence: There is indirect evidence from studies focusing on in situ remelting strategies (e.g., PMC10616214) that control microstructural features, but no clear precedent specifically for dual-laser in situ annealing in this alloy system.
critiques.main_risk: The added system complexity may negate the benefit of a single intervention, and synchronization issues between the lasers could result in inconsistent annealing and unexpected microstructural inhomogeneities.
critiques.fix: Simplify the approach by integrating a post-laser remelting pass using a single laser with controlled power modulation, thereby reducing system complexity while still achieving localized annealing.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach directly addresses the root cause by converting the beam profile to a flat-top shape, thereby reducing localized energy peaks and thermal gradients that generate residual stresses.
critiques.constraints: It is well aligned with the material system and miniature component geometry under LPBF, provided that the beam shaping module is integrated without compromising resolution or other process parameters.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; a uniform energy distribution can lead to a more homogeneous melt pool and improved thermal history, which should reduce residual stress.
critiques.feasibility: Laser beam shaping is an established technique in various laser applications, though retrofitting an LPBF system may require precise calibration and hardware modifications.
critiques.evidence: While direct evidence for beam shaping in this specific alloy is not extensively cited, related studies in LPBF (e.g., PMC10616214 and PMC12162345) highlight melt pool uniformity as critical for stress management.
critiques.main_risk: The risk lies in achieving and maintaining an optimal flat-top profile under operational variations; miscalibration might result in under-melting or other defects offsetting the benefits.
critiques.fix: Include a robust in situ beam profile monitoring and feedback system to ensure maintenance of the flat-top profile during processing.
